title: Ecclesiastes 9:1–10
context: The Preacher affirms that the righteous and the wise are in the hand of God, yet no one can read God's favor or disfavor from events. One event, death, comes to all. The living still have hope, while the dead no longer share in what is done under the sun. From this he urges people to enjoy food, drink, marriage, and work wholeheartedly as God's gift. Interpreters read the statements about the dead in different ways. Many read them as describing death from the vantage of life “under the sun,” a perspective the book itself announces, rather than as a full account of the afterlife. The book does not settle questions about the intermediate state, and no attempt is made to settle them here.

verses.text: For all this I laid to my heart, even to explore all this: that the righteous, and the wise, and their works, are in the hand of God; whether it is love or hatred, man doesn’t know it; all is before them.
verses.arminianNotes: The Preacher concludes “that the righteous, and the wise, and their works, are in the hand of God; whether it is love or hatred, man doesn’t know it.” Arminian readers see God’s care over his people, while noting that outward events do not reveal God's favor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers often connect “in the hand of God” with Proverbs 21:1, where “The king’s heart is in the LORD’s hand like the watercourses.” God’s sovereign care is sure, even when people cannot interpret what lies before them. Both traditions hold this ground in common.

verses.text: All things come alike to all. There is one event to the righteous and to the wicked; to the good, to the clean, to the unclean, to him who sacrifices, and to him who doesn’t sacrifice. As is the good, so is the sinner; he who takes an oath, as he who fears an oath.
verses.arminianNotes: “All things come alike to all.” Arminian readers note that the righteous and the wicked, the worshiper and the non-worshiper, all face the same outward end, so moral choice cannot be measured by earthly outcome.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers compare Matthew 5:45, where God “sends rain on the just and the unjust.” Common experience is not a verdict on anyone's standing before God. Both traditions see shared ground here.

verses.text: This is an evil in all that is done under the sun, that there is one event to all. Yes also, the heart of the sons of men is full of evil, and madness is in their heart while they live, and after that they go to the dead.
verses.arminianNotes: “This is an evil in all that is done under the sun.” Arminian readers note that the Preacher joins two facts: death comes to all, and human hearts are full of evil and madness while they live. Death exposes the folly of wasted lives.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the line “the heart of the sons of men is full of evil” as a sober statement of human sinfulness. Life ends, and then “they go to the dead.” The Preacher does not soften either reality.

verses.text: For to him who is joined with all the living there is hope; for a living dog is better than a dead lion.
verses.arminianNotes: The Preacher adds, “for a living dog is better than a dead lion.” Arminian readers see the value of life as a time of opportunity and hope, when people can still act, respond to God, and do good.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the pointed proverb: the despised dog alive is better off than the noble lion dead. While a person lives, “there is hope,” as the verse says. Both traditions treat life as a gift and a time to act.

verses.text: For the living know that they will die, but the dead don’t know anything, neither do they have any more a reward; for their memory is forgotten.
verses.arminianNotes: The verse says, “but the dead don’t know anything” Arminian readers commonly read this from the Preacher's earthly vantage: the dead no longer know or share in events under the sun, receive no earthly reward, and are forgotten. They do not build an afterlife doctrine on it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise usually read it as describing the dead's loss of earthly knowledge, reward, and memory, as in Ecclesiastes 1:11. The book elsewhere says “the spirit returns to God who gave it” (12:7), so it does not settle the afterlife here.

verses.text: Also their love, their hatred, and their envy has perished long ago; neither do they any longer have a portion forever in anything that is done under the sun.
verses.arminianNotes: “Also their love, their hatred, and their envy has perished long ago.” Arminian readers see the end of all earthly passions and involvement. The dead have no more “portion forever in anything that is done under the sun.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the repeated qualifier “under the sun.” The verse describes what death takes away from life in this world. Both traditions take this as a call to value the present life rather than as a full account of what follows death.

verses.text: Go your way—eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart; for God has already accepted your works.
verses.arminianNotes: “Go your way—eat your bread with joy” Arminian readers see a joyful invitation: because life is brief and God has “already accepted your works,” people should receive ordinary gifts with gladness rather than anxiety.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers often read “God has already accepted your works” as God's approval of enjoying his good gifts. Joy is not self-indulgence but grateful acceptance of what he gives. Both traditions treat this joy as shared ground.

verses.text: Let your garments be always white, and don’t let your head lack oil.
verses.arminianNotes: “Let your garments be always white, and don’t let your head lack oil.” Arminian readers see images of festivity and gladness, an outward expression of a life lived in thankful enjoyment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that white garments and oil were signs of celebration and well-being. The Preacher calls for a settled, ongoing joy, not occasional relief from hardship.

verses.text: Live joyfully with the wife whom you love all the days of your life of vanity, which he has given you under the sun, all your days of vanity, for that is your portion in life, and in your labor in which you labor under the sun.
verses.arminianNotes: “Live joyfully with the wife whom you love” Arminian readers see marriage as one of God's chief gifts in a fleeting life, a companionship to be cherished faithfully. They compare Proverbs 5:18, “Rejoice in the wife of your youth.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that this is “your portion in life,” given by God “under the sun.” Even in days of vanity, marriage is a real good from his hand. Both traditions treat this as shared ground.

verses.text: Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might; for there is no work, nor plan, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in Sheol, where you are going.
verses.arminianNotes: “Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might” Arminian readers see a strong call to wholehearted effort now, while opportunity lasts, since there is no work or plan “in Sheol, where you are going.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read Sheol here as the realm of the dead from an earthly view, where earthly work ends. They often compare Colossians 3:23: “whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord” Both traditions agree on the urgency.
